defaults.permitted_development: Across Oxfordshire, a dropped kerb is normally more of a highways process than a pure planning matter because the work crosses public footway or verge. Planning permission can still enter the picture where the access is onto a classified road, where householder rights do not apply, or where the frontage changes go beyond a simple crossover.

rules.height_rules: Across Oxfordshire, dropped-kerb work is controlled more by highway geometry than by a simple height limit. The council will care about levels, gradients and whether boundary features need to come down to maintain visibility.
rules.depth_rules: Across Oxfordshire, the real depth question is practical rather than formula-based: can a vehicle enter and sit inside the site without blocking the footway? Tight front gardens often fail on that point even before wider design issues are considered.
rules.boundary_rules: Across Oxfordshire, a dropped kerb is not just an opening in your wall: it affects the public highway, so street furniture, utilities, trees, drainage and visibility can all shape the answer. Boundary alterations often need to be planned alongside the crossing rather than afterwards.
rules.roof_rules: Across Oxfordshire, there is no separate roof rule for a dropped kerb. The practical equivalent is whether the access works also introduce other structures, such as a covered entrance, taller gate piers or retaining features, which need to be assessed on their own terms.
rules.materials_rules: Across Oxfordshire, materials matter differently here than on a normal householder project. The authority will usually control the kerb and footway construction, while the private driveway behind it should be robust, well-drained and suitable for repeated vehicle loading.

rules.permitted_development: In Oxford, most dropped-kerb schemes are decided first through the highway authority because the crossing sits within the public highway. That does not guarantee the planning position: access onto a classified road, flats, listed buildings or wider frontage alterations can still mean a planning application is needed.

rules.height_rules: A dropped kerb does not have its own building-height rule. What matters is whether the level changes, gradients and any reduction in walls or hedges still produce a safe and workable access.
rules.depth_rules: There is no national planning depth limit, but the access should lead to enough in-curtilage standing space for a vehicle to clear the footway rather than overhang it. Schemes become harder where a car would project onto the pavement or rely on awkward reversing.
rules.boundary_rules: A dropped kerb is not just an opening in your wall: it affects the public highway, so street furniture, utilities, trees, drainage and visibility can all shape the answer. Boundary alterations often need to be planned alongside the crossing rather than afterwards.

rules.materials_rules: For a dropped kerb, the public-highway build-up is normally specified by the council rather than by the homeowner. On the private side of the boundary, choose surfacing that drains well and will not break up or rut under regular vehicle use.

You normally need the council's vehicle-crossing or dropped-kerb consent to cross the public footway or verge, and planning permission can still be needed for access onto a classified road, at flats, or where wider frontage works fall outside ordinary householder rights.

rules.boundary_rules: The crossing itself stays within the public highway, so utilities, street trees, signs, lighting columns and drainage can all affect the design or lead to refusal. Boundary openings and visibility splays often matter as much as the driveway surface behind the kerb.

rules.height_rules: There is no normal householder height allowance for a dropped kerb. The practical checks are kerb and driveway levels, gradients, and whether boundary walls, fences or banks have to be reduced to keep safe sightlines.
rules.depth_rules: There is no national planning depth limit, but the access should lead to enough in-curtilage standing space for a vehicle to clear the footway rather than overhang it. Schemes become harder where a car would project onto the pavement or rely on awkward reversing.
rules.boundary_rules: A dropped kerb is not just an opening in your wall: it affects the public highway, so street furniture, utilities, trees, drainage and visibility can all shape the answer. Boundary alterations often need to be planned alongside the crossing rather than afterwards.
rules.roof_rules: Roof form is not part of a dropped-kerb assessment, but do not ignore linked structures. If the scheme also adds a canopy, car-port edge, gateway feature or retaining work, those pieces are not automatically covered by the crossing approval.
rules.materials_rules: You do not get a householder right to choose the kerb build-up or footway construction yourself: the highway authority usually specifies the crossing detail. Behind the kerb, use a durable surface and drainage layout that can take vehicle loading without washing water onto the pavement or road.

restrictions.article4_notes: Do not assume the highway licence is the only approval needed: Article 4 directions and site-specific conditions can still require a planning application for linked frontage or access works.
